topic.name: Django Fundamentals
topic.tagline: Projects, apps, URLs, middleware, and the request lifecycle.
topic.description: Build a correct mental model of how a request travels through Django. This is the layer that makes debugging, architecture decisions, and the rest of the framework feel predictable instead of magical.

questions.prompt: In Django's MVT pattern, which component typically contains the request-handling logic?
choices: Model
View
Template
Migration
questions.explanation: Django's view handles the request, asks models for data, and chooses a template response. The template handles presentation, and models describe and persist data. Django's 'view' is closer to a controller in classic MVC.

questions.prompt: What does <int:pk> mean in this URL pattern?
choices: The URL must contain the literal text int:pk.
Capture an integer path segment and pass it to the view as pk.
Restrict the view to integer users only.
Create an integer primary key automatically.
questions.explanation: Path converters capture part of the URL. <int:pk> accepts digits only and passes an int named pk. Other common converters include str, slug, uuid, and path.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a Django project and a Django app?
choices: A project is a reusable package; an app is a deployment target.
A project holds settings and URL configuration; an app is a reusable bundle of related features.
They are identical except for their folder name.
An app can contain only models, never views.
questions.explanation: A project is the site-level configuration and composition root. An app is a Python package with related models, views, templates, and migrations that can be reused across projects. One project can contain many apps.

questions.prompt: Which command starts Django's local development server by default?
choices: python manage.py serve
python manage.py runserver
django start --dev
python manage.py collectstatic
questions.explanation: manage.py runserver starts the development server on 127.0.0.1:8000 by default. It is for local development only: it is not hardened, and it does not serve production traffic well.

questions.prompt: What is INSTALLED_APPS in settings.py for?
choices: It declares the apps whose models, templates, and other components Django should load.
It lists every Python package installed in the virtual environment.
It controls which users may log in.
It defines the database tables directly.
questions.explanation: INSTALLED_APPS is Django's application registry. Entries make models discoverable, enable their templates and static files, and wire up app configs. It is not a list of every pip package.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of include() in a root URLconf?
choices: It imports another app's Python modules into settings.
It delegates a URL prefix to another URLconf so apps can own their routes.
It includes static files in the response.
It merges two Django projects into one database.
questions.explanation: include() lets a project URLconf delegate a prefix to an app's urls.py. That keeps routing modular and lets an app be reused under different prefixes. Namespaces such as app_name make reverse lookups unambiguous.

questions.prompt: Why prefer reverse() over hardcoding a path in a view?
choices: reverse() is faster at runtime.
It derives the URL from the route name, so changing the URL pattern does not break callers.
Hardcoded paths cannot contain slashes.
reverse() automatically adds a trailing slash on every response.
questions.explanation: reverse() resolves a named route and its arguments, keeping links and redirects in sync with urls.py. Templates use the {% url %} tag for the same reason. Hardcoded paths quietly rot when routes change.

questions.prompt: In the MIDDLEWARE list, how are requests and responses processed?
choices: Requests go top to bottom; responses go bottom to top.
Requests go bottom to top; responses go top to bottom.
Both always run in the same top-to-bottom order.
Middleware only runs for admin requests.
questions.explanation: Middleware wraps the request/response cycle like an onion. The request phase enters from the top of the list; the response phase unwinds in reverse. That is why security and session middleware usually sit near the top.

questions.prompt: What is the safe job for AppConfig.ready()?
choices: Run migrations automatically.
Perform one-time in-memory registration such as connecting signals or registering checks.
Query models to warm a cache.
Start a production web server.
questions.explanation: ready() runs during app loading, potentially before the database is ready and during management commands. Avoid database queries there. Use it for registration work such as signal handlers; move data access to lazy code or explicit commands.

questions.prompt: Why does runserver serve static files during development but not in production?
choices: Django deletes static files when DEBUG is off.
The development server has a static-file helper; production is expected to use collectstatic and a web server or CDN.
Static files only work with SQLite.
Browsers block static files from production domains.
questions.explanation: runserver automatically serves app static assets when DEBUG is true. Production should run collectstatic, then let a dedicated web server, object store, or CDN serve STATIC_ROOT. Django itself is not optimised to be a static file server.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best describes a normal Django request?
choices: Middleware → URL resolver → view → template rendering → response middleware
URL resolver → middleware → database → template → view
View → middleware → URL resolver → model → response
Template → URL resolver → middleware → view
questions.explanation: For a normal synchronous request, middleware runs first, then URL resolution selects a view. The view builds data, often with models, and returns a response such as a rendered template. Response middleware unwinds in reverse.

questions.prompt: What does app_name = "blog" enable in an included URLconf?
choices: It renames the Python package on disk.
It creates a URL namespace so routes reverse as blog:detail.
It makes the app's URLs private to staff users.
It forces every view to be class-based.
questions.explanation: app_name sets an application namespace. When included with a matching instance namespace, routes reverse as blog:detail. Namespacing prevents collisions when several apps both define a detail route.

questions.prompt: Why should startup code avoid hitting the database in AppConfig.ready()?
choices: Django has no database connection during ready().
ready() can run before migrations are applied and during commands that should not touch the database.
Database queries in ready() are always cached forever.
ready() runs once per request, making it too slow.
questions.explanation: App loading happens for migrate, makemigrations, and management commands, sometimes before the schema exists. A query in ready() can crash a fresh setup or make commands unexpectedly slow. Prefer lazy access or explicit management commands.

questions.prompt: What is the practical difference between WSGI and ASGI in Django?
choices: WSGI is asynchronous; ASGI is synchronous.
WSGI is a synchronous request/response interface; ASGI also supports async views, WebSockets, and long-lived connections.
ASGI replaces the ORM.
Only WSGI can run on Windows.
questions.explanation: WSGI handles one synchronous request at a time per worker. ASGI is an asynchronous interface and can support WebSockets, HTTP/2, and long-lived connections. Django supports both; choose based on the server and features you need.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Django signals is most accurate?
choices: Signals are a replacement for model methods and should handle all business rules.
Signals decouple senders from receivers, but implicit control flow can make behaviour harder to trace and test.
Signals run in a separate database transaction by default.
A signal receiver can only be connected in settings.py.
questions.explanation: Signals are useful for cross-cutting notifications, but they hide dependencies and can fire in surprising contexts such as tests, fixtures, or bulk operations. Prefer explicit service functions or model methods for core business rules; use signals sparingly.

flashcards.front: Explain Django's MVT architecture in one minute.
flashcards.back: Model: data structure and persistence. View: receives a request, applies logic, fetches data, and returns a response. Template: presentation layer that renders data. Django's URLconf connects paths to views. MVT is MVC with the framework handling the controller role.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a Django project and an app?
flashcards.back: A project is the site-level container: settings, root URLconf, WSGI/ASGI entry points. An app is a reusable package of features: models, views, templates, migrations. A project can include many apps, and an app can be reused in other projects.
flashcards.front_code:
django-admin startproject config .
python manage.py startapp shop

flashcards.front: How do path converters work in Django URLs?
flashcards.back: A converter captures part of the path and validates its type. <int:pk> captures digits and passes an int. Use <slug:slug>, <uuid:id>, <str:name>, or <path:rest>. The captured value arrives as a keyword argument to the view.

flashcards.front: Why use reverse() and {% url %} instead of hardcoded paths?
flashcards.back: They resolve URLs from route names and parameters, so a change to urls.py propagates everywhere automatically. Hardcoded paths break silently. reverse() is for Python code; {% url %} is the template equivalent.

flashcards.front: What does middleware do, and in which order does it run?
flashcards.back: Middleware is a layered wrapper around the request/response cycle. Requests run through MIDDLEWARE top to bottom; responses unwind bottom to top. It is suitable for sessions, auth, CSRF, security headers, and cross-cutting request concerns.

flashcards.front: When would you choose ASGI over WSGI?
flashcards.back: Choose ASGI when you need WebSockets, long-lived connections, HTTP/2, or genuinely concurrent async I/O. For an ordinary server-rendered CRUD app, WSGI with a well-run sync server is still a perfectly good choice. ASGI does not make slow blocking code fast.
flashcards.front_code:
# wsgi.py -> WSGI application
# asgi.py -> ASGI application

flashcards.front: What is safe to do in AppConfig.ready()?
flashcards.back: Use ready() for in-memory registration: connecting signals, registering system checks, or wiring up plugin hooks. Do not query models or assume migrations have run. Startup code can execute during migrate and management commands.
